doc.title: Rossano Sportiello interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, October 2, 2015 [interview 1 of 2]

title: His one classical piano teacher
summary: His single teacher from age 9 to 22 never objected to jazz and, late in life, enjoyed learning Rhapsody in Blue.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Right. It’s pretty profound. Did you have professors or piano teachers — the classical piano teachers, did they make an issue of you being a jazz player at the same time?

I had only one classical piano teacher. From the beginning, I was age 9 until the final graduation at age 22, and he never was difficult that way. He always let me do what I wanted as far as I would practice also the regular stuff. I mean Beethoven and Chopin and Bach and so on. And as a matter of fact I think that he was also interested, mildly interested, in jazz. But somehow the way he was brought up was too far away from the mentality of a jazz pianist improvising. But I think that inside he might have thought I wish I could do that. In fact, shortly before he passed away one day I went to see him on one of my trips in Italy a few years ago. And he said, “you know it’s been a couple of years that I was fooling around with ‘Rhapsody in Blue’ by Gershwin.” That of course is not jazz, but among the so-called classical repertoire it’s one of those pieces that goes in that direction. And so he said, “finally now I understood the piece and I’m enjoying it. I’m enjoying the harmony.” And so I felt my goodness, finally he made it to the other side. And then a couple of months after that unfortunately he passed away.
Oh. Well I’m glad he had that experience. It sort of opened his ears a little bit.
